Unlike [CP Decomposition](2255-cp-decomposition.md), which uses a sum of rank-one components (outer products of pure vectors), VM uses a sum of vector-matrix outer products, effectively acting as a special case of Block Term Decomposition (BTD) [S2][S4, unofficial].

The evidence in both Source [S2] and Source [S4] explicitly states that VM decomposition uses a sum of vector-matrix outer products, unlike CP decomposition which uses a sum of outer products of pure vectors. Both sources also confirm that VM is effectively a special case of Block Term Decomposition (BTD).
supported
This trade-off increases the model size per component compared to CP but significantly reduces the required number of components $R$ for the same expression capacity [S2][S4, unofficial].

The evidence in both Source [S2] and Source [S4] explicitly states that Vector-Matrix (VM) decomposition increases the model size per component compared to CP decomposition (which uses pure vectors). Simultaneously, both sources confirm that this trade-off allows each component to express more complex data, thereby significantly reducing the required number of components ($R$) for the same expression capacity.
supported

Vector-Matrix (VM) decomposition is a tensor factorization technique that reduces the memory footprint of high-dimensional data by factorizing a tensor into a sum of vector-matrix outer products [S2][S4, unofficial].

The claim states that Vector-Matrix (VM) decomposition is a tensor factorization technique that reduces memory footprint by factorizing a tensor into a sum of vector-matrix outer products. The evidence from Source [S2] and Source [S4] explicitly confirms this: both sources define VM decomposition as factorizing a tensor into a sum of vector-matrix outer products (unlike CP which uses pure vectors) and state that this approach reduces memory complexity from O(N^3) to O(N^2), thereby reducing the memory footprint.
supported

*   **Limitations:** Increases model size per component compared to pure vector-based factorization in CP [S2][S4, unofficial].

The claim states that the evidence supports the limitation that the method increases model size per component compared to pure vector-based factorization in CP. Both Source [S2] and Source [S4] explicitly state this fact. For instance, S2 notes: 'While this increases the model size compared to pure vector-based factorization in CP...' and S4 notes: 'Note that, each of our component tensors has more parameters than a component in CP decomposition.' Therefore, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.

VM decomposition was inspired by CP decomposition and Block Term Decomposition (BTD) [S4, unofficial].

The source text explicitly states in multiple places that VM decomposition is 'inspired by the CP and block term decomposition [13]' and that it can be seen as a 'special case of general BTD'. The claim accurately reflects these statements found in the evidence.
supported
*   **Time Complexity:** TensoRF with VM decomposition achieves reconstruction time of less than 10 minutes, which is about 100x faster than NeRF [S2][S4, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states in Source [S2] that 'TensoRF with VM decomposition further boosts rendering quality... while reducing the reconstruction time (< 10 min)' and that this is 'significantly faster (about 100x) than NeRF'. This directly supports the claim regarding the time complexity and speed comparison.
supported

*   **When Not to Use:** When extreme compactness per component is prioritized over expression capacity, or when the scene has highly anisotropic complexity that cannot be well-approximated by the symmetric $R_1=R_2=R_3$ assumption [S2][S4, unofficial].

The evidence in Source [S2] and Source [S4] explicitly supports both conditions mentioned in the claim. First, regarding 'extreme compactness per component', the sources state that VM decomposition 'increases model size compared to pure vector-based factorization in CP' (S2, S4), implying that if one prioritizes the compactness of individual components over total model size or expression capacity, CP would be preferred over VM. Second, regarding 'anisotropic complexity', Source [S4] notes that 'R1, R2, R3 can be set differently and should be chosen depending on the complexity of each mode,' and that the symmetric assumption ($R_1=R_2=R_3$) is used for scenes that 'appear equally complex along its three axes.' This implies that for scenes with highly anisotropic complexity (unequal complexity along axes), the symmetric assumption is not well-suited, and the general form with different $R_i$ values is required. Thus, the claim accurately reflects the trade-offs and assumptions described in the evidence.
supported
The number of decomposed components for the density grid, $N_\sigma$, is typically 16 [S6].
The source text explicitly states in the experimental setup section: 'The number of decomposed components Nσ = 16 and Na = 48.' This directly confirms the claim that Nσ is typically 16.

This allows each component to express more complex tensor data of higher ranks compared to pure vector-based CP decomposition [S2][S4, unofficial].

The claim states that the decomposition allows each component to express more complex tensor data of higher ranks compared to pure vector-based CP decomposition. Both Source [S2] and Source [S4] explicitly state this. For instance, S2 notes: 'we enable each component to express more complex tensor data of higher ranks, thus significantly reducing the required number of components.' Similarly, S4 states: 'a VM component tensor can express more complex high-dimensional data than a CP component.' The claim accurately reflects the information provided in the evidence.
supported

*   **When to Use:** When high rendering quality is required with fast reconstruction times and compact memory footprint, and the scene complexity is relatively uniform across axes [S2][S4, unofficial].

The claim states that VM decomposition is used when high rendering quality, fast reconstruction, compact memory, and uniform scene complexity are required. The evidence supports all these points: [S2] and [S4] explicitly state that VM decomposition boosts rendering quality and achieves fast reconstruction (<10 min) with a compact model size (<75 MB). Furthermore, both sources note that for scenes with equal complexity along axes (uniform complexity), the number of components is set equally ($R_1=R_2=R_3=R$), which aligns with the 'uniform across axes' condition in the claim.
supported

Features stored in these factors are typically decoded by an MLP to produce final values (e.g., density and color) [S1].

Additionally, the notes confirm: 'Stores vectors v and matrices M instead of direct density/color. Features are decoded by an MLP.' This directly supports the claim.

It was proposed by Chen et al. in the TensoRF paper [S2][S4, unofficial][S5, unofficial].

The claim states that the VM decomposition was proposed by Chen et al. in the TensoRF paper. The provided evidence from sources [S2], [S4], and [S5] (which are excerpts from the TensoRF paper) explicitly introduces the 'novel vector-matrix (VM) decomposition' as part of the TensoRF framework. The text describes the technique, its mathematical formulation, and its benefits, confirming that this specific decomposition method is the core proposal of the TensoRF paper authored by Chen et al.
